segments.translit: paramakaruṇāarjjaṇāya tam evārthaṃ abhijñālābhī jayanandipādaḥ pratipādayati—
segments.translation: For the gathering of supreme [compassion]{karuna}, [Jayanandipāda]{p-jayanandi}, who has gained the [higher knowledges]{abhijna}, sets out that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song (cp.46.m1): Jayanandipāda, who has gained the higher knowledges, sets out 'that same meaning' for the sake of gathering supreme compassion. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don) where the Sanskrit has 'that same meaning' (tam evārthaṃ).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', where the Sanskrit has tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning', as if reading tattvārthaṃ. Translated as printed.

paramakaruṇāarjjaṇāya (printed without sandhi, for paramakaruṇārjanāya): 'for the gathering (or earning) of supreme compassion'. The Tibetan agrees (mchog gi snying rje bsags pa'i phyir). Whose compassion it is, and for whom it is gathered, is not said.

segments.translit:
pekhai ityādi| yathā svapne svapratibhāsa[ṃ] yathādarśe pratibimbaṃ tādṛśam antarā bhavavijñānaṃ paśya|
tathā cāgamaḥ|—
jima jalamajhe caṃda sa hi nosa ityādi|
segments.translation:
'See…' and so on. As in a [dream]{svapna} one's own [appearance]{abhasa}, as in a [mirror]{mirror} a [reflection]{pratibimba}: just so, see the [consciousness]{vijnana} of the [intermediate existence]{antarabhava}.
And so the [scripture]{agama} says:
'Like the [moon in water]{udakacandra}, it neither is nor is not…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta applies the dream and the mirror image to consciousness 'in between' (cp.46.m2). His antarā bhavavijñāna, which the Tibetan reads as consciousness of the intermediate existence (bar srid), implies that the song's in-between is the state between death and rebirth, and that what is like a dream or a reflection is that consciousness. He does not mention delusion.

citations.quoted: jima jalamajhe caṃda sa hi nosa (Like the moon in water, it neither is nor is not…)
citations.work: unnamed scripture (āgama; Tibetan lung), an Apabhraṃśa verse, not identified

flags.note: Shastri prints antarā bhavavijñānaṃ as two words. I read one compound, antarābhavavijñānaṃ, 'consciousness of the intermediate existence', as the Tibetan does (bar srid kyi rnam par shes pa); spacing in the edition is editorial. As printed it would be 'in between, see the consciousness of existence'. Either way he puts antarā where the song has antarāle, and he has no word for the song's moha.

The Tibetan line of 1b reads bar gyi srid pa nyid kyang de bzhin no, 'the intermediate existence too is like that', with no word for delusion. It agrees with Munidatta's paraphrase rather than with the draft's 'so is delusion in the in-between'.
For svapratibhāsa[ṃ], 'one's own appearance' in a dream, the Tibetan has rmi lam gyi skyes bu, 'the person in a dream'.

The quoted line is clear up to caṃda ('as the moon in the midst of water'); sa hi nosa does not construe as printed. 'It neither is nor is not' follows the Tibetan, yod med min. The words may be a damaged sāca ṇa mosa, 'neither true nor false', the phrase the glossary records with the same image in song 29 (4b).

Munidatta cites the opening as pekhai (a present form) where the song has pekhu, but paraphrases with the imperative paśya; the Tibetan cites blta bar gyis, 'look!', as in its line. Rendered 'See…' to match the draft.

segments.translit:
bho anadhigata(taṃ)mārga yadi tvaṃ vijñānasaṃkramaṇakāle 'pi sadguruvacanamārgam anusmaran svacitta[ṃ] mohavimuktaṃ karoṣi tadabhāve saṃsāre yātāyātaṃ truṭyati| tasmāt svātmānaṃ mithyārthe(he) na kimarthaṃ niṣphalaṃ bādhayase|
tathā ca bhusukupādāḥ|
kleśā viṣayeṣv ityādi—
segments.translation:
O you who have not understood the [path]{marga}: if even at the time of the passing of [consciousness]{vijnana} you call to mind the [path]{marga} of the true [guru's word]{guru-vacana} and make your own [mind]{citta} free of [delusion]{moha}, then in its absence [coming and going]{coming-and-going} in [saṃsāra]{samsara} breaks off. So why do you fruitlessly torment yourself with what is false?
And so [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says:
'The [afflictions]{klesa}, in the [sense objects]{visaya}…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as counsel for the moment of death (cp.46.m3): if, even as consciousness passes on, you recall the true guru's word and free your own mind from delusion, coming and going in saṃsāra breaks off. The mind of 2a is thus one's own, and the coming and going of 2b is coming and going in saṃsāra.

citations.quoted: kleśā viṣayeṣu… (The afflictions, in the sense objects…)
citations.work: a verse of Bhusukupāda (named by Munidatta; the work is not named)

flags.note: vijñānasaṃkramaṇa is the passing of consciousness at death (Tibetan rnam par shes pas yang dag par 'gro ba), not saṃkrama, 'bridge'. niṣphalaṃ is 'fruitlessly' (Tibetan 'bras bu med pa), not the glossary's 'fruit' (phala). Neither is marked as those entries. If the passing of consciousness recurs, it may deserve an entry of its own.

mithyārthe(he) na does not construe as printed: the na is stranded. I read mithyārthena, 'with what is false', taking the space as editorial; Shastri's (he) suggests another reading of the syllable. The Tibetan has log par rmongs pas, 'through false delusion', as if mithyāmohena, and takes svātmānaṃ as 'about your own nature' (rang gi ngo bo nyid la).

bho anadhigata(taṃ)mārga is a vocative, 'O you who have not understood the path'; Shastri's (taṃ) marks a doubtful syllable without changing the sense. The Tibetan makes it a condition: 'if you have not understood the path' (gal te khyod kyis lam ma rtogs na).
The Tibetan has no 'path' in 'the path of the true guru's word' (bla ma dam pa'i gsung rjes su dran pas), and turns 'you make your mind free of delusion' into a command (khyod gyis shig).

kleśāviṣayeṣv is divided kleśā viṣayeṣu, 'the afflictions, in the sense objects', as the Tibetan takes it (nyon mongs yul rnams la); kleśa-aviṣayeṣu is also possible. The comment cites none of the refrain's words; its place on couplet 2 rests on mohavimuktaṃ and yātāyātaṃ truṭyati, which echo 2a and 2b.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena paramātmacittasyānu[64ka]śaṃsām āha—
no dāṭai ityādi| sadgurucaraṇapaṅkajarajaḥprasaṅgāt tad evaṃ saṃsāramano yadi mohavimuktaṃ bhavati| tadāgninā na dagdhaṃ bhavati| jale na plāvanīyaṃ bhavati| śastreṇa cchettuṃ na pāryyate| paramārthacittasyāṅkam adaḥ(daṃ)| evaṃ paśyan san tathāpi kudhiyo mohe paraṃ baddhā bhavanti|
tathā ca bahiśāstre—
yatnena pāryyāṇi samācaranti puṇyaprasaṅgād api * * * *|
āścaryyam etad dhi manuṣyaloke kṣīraṃ parityajya viṣaṃ pibanti(ta)||
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the [mind]{citta} that is the supreme self:
'It is not [burnt]{burning}…' and so on. If in this way, through contact with the dust of the true [guru]{guru}'s [lotus]{lotus} feet, that [mind]{citta} of [saṃsāra]{samsara} becomes free of [delusion]{moha}, then it is not [burnt]{burning} by [fire]{fire}, it cannot be [wetted]{wetting} in [water]{water}, and it cannot be [cut]{cutting} with a weapon. This is the mark of the [ultimate]{paramartha} mind. Even seeing this, the dull-witted are utterly bound in [delusion]{moha}.
And so in an [outer treatise]{bahyasastra}:
'With effort they practise sins; even when merit comes their way … .
This is a [wonder]{adbhuta} in the world of men: giving up [milk]{milk}, they drink [poison]{visa}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3 as praise of the ultimate mind (cp.46.m4): freed from delusion by the dust of the guru's feet, it cannot be burnt, wetted or cut. The draft follows his paraphrase of 3b, 'even seeing this, the dull-witted are utterly bound in delusion'. The Tibetan line reads moa as illusion and bali bali as white hair and wrinkles.

equations.src: no dāṭai (3a: not burnt, not wetted, not cut)
equations.en: the mark of the ultimate mind (paramārthacitta), freed from delusion

citations.quoted: yatnena pāryyāṇi samācaranti puṇyaprasaṅgād api * * * * | āścaryyam etad dhi manuṣyaloke kṣīraṃ parityajya viṣaṃ pibanti (With effort they practise sins… giving up milk, they drink poison)
citations.work: an 'outer treatise' (bahiśāstra; Tibetan phyi'i bstan bcos), apparently non-Buddhist, not identified

flags.note: Bearing on 3b: Munidatta's paraphrase (evaṃ paśyan san tathāpi kudhiyo mohe paraṃ baddhā bhavanti) takes moa as fools and bali bali as an intensive, as the draft does. The Tibetan line, sgyu ma la rmongs skra dkar gnyer 'jigs ltos, reads moa as illusion (sgyu ma) and the doubled bali as white hair and wrinkles (compare Sanskrit palita, valī).
pāryyāṇi in the quoted verse gives no clear sense. 'Sins' follows the Tibetan sdig pa, as if pāpāni, which the contrast with merit in the next words also suits.

The manuscript has a gap (* * * *) after puṇyaprasaṅgād api. The Tibetan fills it: bsod nams zhar la byung yang spyod mi byed, 'even when merit comes their way by chance, they do not practise it'. The translation keeps the gap as an ellipsis.

For paramātmacitta, 'the mind that is the supreme self', the Tibetan has don dam pa'i sems, 'ultimate mind', as if paramārthacitta, the word Munidatta uses a few lines on; paramātma- may be a slip. Translated as printed.

paramārthacittasyāṅkam adaḥ(daṃ): 'this is the mark of the ultimate mind' (Shastri's (daṃ) points to idaṃ). The Tibetan has don dam pa'i sems rtags kyi nga rgyal, 'pride in the mark of the ultimate mind', apparently reading aṅka-mada.

The Tibetan calls this the third verse (rkang pa gsum pa) where the Sanskrit has dvitīyapada, 'second verse'; on the next couplet it has 'second' (rkang pa gnyis pa) for tṛtīyapada, so its numbering here looks confused.
jale na plāvanīyaṃ means 'cannot be flooded, swept away, by water'; the Tibetan has chus khyer ba, 'carried off by water'. 'Wetted' follows the glossary's 'wet' for the entry wetting.
The folio mark [৬৪ক] falls inside anuśaṃsām and is translated through. Munidatta cites the line as no dāṭai where the song has nau. The singular paśyan san sits loosely with the plural kudhiyaḥ.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena paramārthasatyasya lakṣaṇa[m]—
chāyetyādi| mohavimuktā yadā paramārthavido bhavanti| tadā chāyāmāyāsamaṃ svavigrahaṃ jñānalocanena paśyanti(ti) pakṣāpakṣabhinnaṃ śrīherukarūpaṃ cākalayanti(ti)|
tathaca sarahapādāḥ—
mahāmāyādevītyādi|—
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada}, the defining mark of [ultimate]{paramartha} truth:
'[Shade]{shade}…' and so on. When, freed from [delusion]{moha}, they come to know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, then with the [eye]{eye} of [knowledge]{jnana} they see their own [body]{body} as like [shade]{shade} and [illusion]{maya}, and they perceive the form of glorious [Heruka]{p-heruka}, distinct from [side]{paksa} and non-side.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
'The [goddess]{devi} [Mahāmāyā]{p-mahamaya}…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 4 as the mark of ultimate truth (cp.46.m5): freed from delusion, those who know the ultimate see their own body as like shade and illusion, and perceive Heruka's form 'distinct from side and non-side'. That takes 4b's biṇā as vinā, 'without', as the draft does; he says nothing of a vīṇā. He cites Saraha on Mahāmāyā.

citations.work: a verse of Saraha (named by Munidatta; the work is not named)

flags.note: pakṣāpakṣabhinnaṃ, 'distinct from side and non-side'. The Tibetan has phyogs dang phyogs ma yin pa dbyer med pa, 'with side and non-side inseparable', as if abhinna (a sandhi pakṣāpakṣābhinnaṃ, with long ā, would give that). The two senses are opposite, and they bear on 4b: Munidatta's supports 'without both sides', the Tibetan's would not.

Where the Sanskrit has śrīherukarūpaṃ, 'the form of glorious Heruka', the Tibetan has dpal he ru ka lnga, 'the five glorious Herukas'. It also lacks 'shade' (only sgyu ma dang 'dra bar, 'like an illusion') and divides jñānalocana into 'knowing' and 'with the eye' (shes nas mig gis).
The Tibetan calls this the second verse (rkang pa gnyis pa) where the Sanskrit has tṛtīyapada, 'third verse'.

mohavimuktā yadā paramārthavido bhavanti can mean 'when the knowers of the ultimate are freed from delusion' or 'when, freed from delusion, they come to know the ultimate'; the second follows the Tibetan (gti mug las grol ba gang gi tshe don dam par rig par 'gyur). Shastri's (ti) after paśyanti and ākalayanti marks a doubtful syllable, perhaps singular forms, without changing the sense. tathaca is printed for tathā ca.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena cittaphalasvarūpam āha—
tatheti| prajñāpāramitārthamahārasena cittavāsanādoṣaviśodhanaṃ yadi kriyate budhaiḥ| tadā jayanandipādo hi vadati| cittam anyathābhāvaṃ na bhavati| tathatāviśu[65]ddho hi yaḥ sa tathāparaṃ bhavati|
tathā ca śrīdvikalparāje—
sarvveṣāṃ khalu vastūnāṃ viśuddhis tathata matā|| 46||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of the [fruit]{phala} of [mind]{citta}:
'[Suchness]{tathata}…' and so on. If the wise, with the [great essence]{maharasa} of the meaning of the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}, carry out the [purification]{visuddhi} of the faults of the mind's [habitual tendencies]{vasana}, then, [Jayanandipāda]{p-jayanandi} says, the [mind]{citta} does not become otherwise. For whoever is [purified]{visuddhi} in [suchness]{tathata} becomes wholly such.
And so in the glorious [Dvikalparāja]{tx-hevajra}:
'The [purity]{visuddhi} of all things, indeed, is held to be [suchness]{tathata}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as the fruit of mind (cp.46.m6): when the wise purify the mind's habitual tendencies with the great essence of the perfection of wisdom, 'the mind does not become otherwise'. He thus takes 5b's aṇa as anya, 'other', with the mind as subject, and has no clear word for phuḍa, 'plainly'.

citations.quoted: sarvveṣāṃ khalu vastūnāṃ viśuddhis tathata matā (The purity of all things, indeed, is held to be suchness)
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (cited as śrīdvikalparāja; Tibetan brtag pa gnyis pa)

flags.note: Bearing on 5b: Munidatta's cittam anyathābhāvaṃ na bhavati takes aṇa ṇa hoi as 'does not become other', with the mind as subject, and has no word for phuḍa unless his emphatic hi stands for it. The Tibetan line has gsal byed gzhan min no, 'the illuminator is not other', apparently taking phuḍa (sphuṭa, 'clear') as the subject.

sa tathāparaṃ bhavati can be divided tathā paraṃ, 'becomes wholly such' (chosen), or tathā aparaṃ, which gives no clear sense. The Tibetan sets the sentence as verse, rnam dag de bzhin nyid gang las / de nyid gzhan du ma yin no, 'that which is pure suchness is not otherwise', echoing the 'not other' of 5b.
The Tibetan comment splits anyathābhāvaṃ: sems ni gzhan ma yin te dngos po med pa ma yin no, 'the mind is not other; it is not nonexistent', as if anyathā + abhāva.

The lemma is printed tatheti (tathā iti), apparently for the song's tathātā; the Tibetan cites sems kyi … de nyid, 'of mind… suchness'. Rendered 'Suchness…' to match the draft. The folio mark [৬৫] inside viśuddho is translated through, and the song number || 46 || is not translated.

In the Dvikalpa verse the Tibetan (dngos rnams kun gyi nges pa ni / rnam dag de bzhin nyid du 'dod) renders khalu as nges pa, 'the certainty of all things', and makes viśuddhi qualify suchness: 'is held to be pure suchness'. The printed tathata stands for tathatā. The title is kept as he gives it, Dvikalparāja, and linked to the Hevajra entry.

questions: 1b: Munidatta (cp.46.m2) and the Tibetan line (bar gyi srid pa nyid kyang de bzhin no) both take antarāle as the intermediate existence between death and rebirth, and neither has a word for delusion. Should 1b keep 'so is delusion in the in-between', and should antarala stay 'in-between' or point to antarabhava ('intermediate existence')?

cp.46.m2: is the compound reading antarābhavavijñāna (Tibetan bar srid kyi rnam par shes pa), against Shastri's spacing antarā bhavavijñānaṃ, acceptable? And the rendering of the unclear 'sa hi nosa' after the Tibetan yod med min ('it neither is nor is not')?
cp.46.m4: the glossary's 'wet' (wetting) is used for plāvanīya, which means 'flooded, swept away' (Tibetan chus khyer ba). Keep 'wetted', or allow 'flooded' in the commentary?

cp.46.m4: 'sins' for pāryyāṇi follows the Tibetan sdig pa. Should the gap after puṇyaprasaṅgād api stay an ellipsis, or be filled from the Tibetan ('they do not practise it') with the flag as warrant?

4b: Munidatta's pakṣāpakṣabhinna ('distinct from side and non-side') supports 'without both sides' (biṇā as vinā) and gives no ground for vīṇā; but the Tibetan comment's dbyer med ('inseparable') and the Tibetan line ('in the two sides one sees variety') read otherwise. Keep the draft, with a witness note on the line?

5b: the Tibetan line (gsal byed gzhan min no, 'the illuminator is not other') takes phuḍa as the subject, where Munidatta makes the mind the subject and does not gloss phuḍa. Does the draft's 'plainly' need a note?
cp.46.m6: tathāparaṃ read as tathā paraṃ, 'becomes wholly such'. Acceptable, or would you prefer a rendering after the Tibetan ('is not otherwise')?
